passages.text: Glucocorticoid Repression of Inflammatory Gene Expression Shows Differential Responsiveness by Transactivation- and Transrepression-Dependent Mechanisms

Binding of glucocorticoid to the glucocorticoid receptor (GR/NR3C1) may repress inflammatory gene transcription via direct, protein synthesis-independent processes (transrepression), or by activating transcription (transactivation) of multiple anti-inflammatory/repressive factors. <sentence_start/>Using human pulmonary A549 cells, we showed that 34 out of 39 IL-1β-inducible mRNAs were repressed to varying degrees by the synthetic glucocorticoid, dexamethasone. <sentence_start/>Whilst these repressive effects were GR-dependent, they did not correlate with either the magnitude of IL-1β-inducibility or the NF-κB-dependence of the inflammatory genes. <sentence_start/>This suggests that induction by IL-1β and repression by dexamethasone are independent events. <sentence_start/>Roles for transactivation were investigated using the protein synthesis inhibitor, cycloheximide. <sentence_start/>However, cycloheximide reduced the IL-1β-dependent expression of 13 mRNAs, which, along with the 5 not showing repression by dexamethasone, were not analysed further. <sentence_start/>Of the remaining 21 inflammatory mRNAs, cycloheximide significantly attenuated the dexamethasone-dependent repression of 11 mRNAs that also showed a marked time-dependence to their repression. <sentence_start/>Such effects are consistent with repression occurring via the <italic toggle="yes">de novo</italic> synthesis of a new product, or products, which subsequently cause repression (i.e., repression via a transactivation mechanism). <sentence_start/>Conversely, 10 mRNAs showed completely cycloheximide-independent, and time-independent, repression by dexamethasone. <sentence_start/>This is consistent with direct GR transrepression. <sentence_start/>Importantly, the inflammatory mRNAs showing attenuated repression by dexamethasone in the presence of cycloheximide also showed a significantly greater extent of repression and a higher potency to dexamethasone compared to those mRNAs showing cycloheximide-independent repression. <sentence_start/>This suggests that the repression of inflammatory mRNAs by GR transactivation-dependent mechanisms accounts for the greatest levels of repression and the most potent repression by dexamethasone. <sentence_start/>In conclusion, our data indicate roles for both transrepression and transactivation in the glucocorticoid-dependent repression of inflammatory gene expression. <sentence_start/>However, transactivation appears to account for the more potent and efficacious mechanism of repression by glucocorticoids on these IL-1β-induced genes.
Introduction

Glucocorticoids acting on the glucocorticoid receptor (GR/NR3C1) are the most effective anti-inflammatory drugs available for multiple inflammatory conditions <citation rid="pone.0053936-Barnes1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16436275" doi="10.1016/j.ejphar.2005.12.052" count="1">[1]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Thus, inhaled glucocorticoids reduce lung inflammation and are consequently recommended for all but the mildest asthmatics <citation rid="pone.0053936-Barnes1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16436275" doi="10.1016/j.ejphar.2005.12.052" count="1">[1]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0053936-Newton1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="19932713" doi="10.1016/j.pharmthera.2009.11.003" count="1">[2]</citation>. <sentence_start/>The profound anti-inflammatory effects of these drugs are largely derived from their ability to repress the expression of numerous inflammatory genes <citation rid="pone.0053936-Newton2" ref-type="bibr" pmid="10856322" doi="10.1136/thorax.55.7.603" pmcid="PMC1745805" count="1">[3]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0053936-Rhen1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16236742" doi="10.1056/NEJMra050541" count="1">[4]</citation>. <sentence_start/>While the classical paradigm of action for nuclear hormone receptors, such as GR, is to activate gene transcription from hormone response elements, e.g. palindromic glucocorticoid response elements (GREs), this has not generally been thought to explain repression of inflammatory gene expression <citation rid="pone.0053936-Barnes1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16436275" doi="10.1016/j.ejphar.2005.12.052" count="1">[1]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0053936-Rhen1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16236742" doi="10.1056/NEJMra050541" count="1">[4]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Rather this is attributed to multiple mechanisms of which transrepression, the ability of GR to directly repress gene transcription, is prominent <citation rid="pone.0053936-DeBosscher1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="12920152" doi="10.1210/er.2002-0006" count="1">[5]</citation>. <sentence_start/>In the transrepression hypothesis <citation rid="pone.0053936-Clark1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="22212616" doi="10.1016/j.pharmthera.2011.12.004" count="1">[6]</citation>, ligand-activated GR interacts with, or tethers to, key transcription factors, such as NF-κB and AP-1, to switch off inflammatory gene transcription. <sentence_start/>GR may then recruit histone deacetylases (HDACs), in particular HDAC2 <citation rid="pone.0053936-Ito1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="10958685" doi="10.1128/mcb.20.18.6891-6903.2000" pmcid="PMC88765" count="1">[7]</citation>, to the promoters of inflammatory genes and thereby exert repression, in part, via effects on the local chromatin environment <citation rid="pone.0053936-Barnes2" ref-type="bibr" pmid="21198556" doi="10.1111/j.1476-5381.2010.01199.x" pmcid="PMC3085866" count="1">[8]</citation>. <sentence_start/>However, transrepression has also been explained by competition for co-activator molecules and GR-dependent changes in RNA polymerase II phosphorylation <citation rid="pone.0053936-Ray1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="8290595" doi="10.1073/pnas.91.2.752" pmcid="PMC43027" count="1">[9]</citation>-<citation rid="pone.0053936-Luecke1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15879558" doi="10.1101/gad.1297105" pmcid="PMC1091745" count="1">[11]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Equally, a dramatic glucocorticoid-dependent up-regulation of IκBα (NFKBIA), the endogenous inhibitor of NF-κB, was indicated as a major driver of glucocorticoid repression <citation rid="pone.0053936-Auphan1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="7569976" doi="10.1126/science.270.5234.286" count="1">[12]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0053936-Scheinman1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="7569975" doi="10.1126/science.270.5234.283" count="1">[13]</citation>. <sentence_start/>However, many investigators have not observed such substantial effects and transcriptional repression of inflammatory genes can be dissociated from glucocorticoid-dependent increases in NFKBIA expression <citation rid="pone.0053936-Brostjan1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="8702657" doi="10.1074/jbc.271.32.19612" count="1">[14]</citation>-<citation rid="pone.0053936-Heck1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="9303314" doi="10.1093/emboj/16.15.4698" pmcid="PMC1170096" count="1">[17]</citation>. <sentence_start/>While other repressive mechanisms include GR binding to negative GREs (nGREs) in genes such as prolactin or proopiomelanocortin (POMC) <citation rid="pone.0053936-Sakai1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="3192076" doi="10.1101/gad.2.9.1144" count="1">[18]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0053936-Drouin1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="2586521" doi="10.1128/mcb.9.12.5305" pmcid="PMC363695" count="1">[19]</citation>, a lack of readily definable nGRE sites in the promoters of inflammatory genes argued against this mechanism of repression <citation rid="pone.0053936-DeBosscher1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="12920152" doi="10.1210/er.2002-0006" count="1">[5]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Indeed, direct nGRE-dependent repression of POMC is probably described by tethering type interactions of GR at the promoter sites required for transcriptional activation <citation rid="pone.0053936-Bilodeau1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="17043312" doi="10.1101/gad.1444606" pmcid="PMC1619949" count="1">[20]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Equally, GR chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) experiments combined with genomic PCR, microarray (ChIP-chip) or high throughput sequencing (ChIP-SEQ) analyses primarily revealed GR binding sites at glucocorticoid-induced rather than repressed gene promoters <citation rid="pone.0053936-Wang1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15501915" doi="10.1073/pnas.0407008101" pmcid="PMC524211" count="1">[21]</citation>-<citation rid="pone.0053936-Reddy1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="19801529" doi="10.1101/gr.097022.109" pmcid="PMC2792167" count="1">[23]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Despite this, a more recent study has again raised the issue of nGREs as a widespread mechanism of repression <citation rid="pone.0053936-Surjit1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="21496643" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2011.03.027" count="1">[24]</citation>. <sentence_start/>While the degree to which these mechanisms apply in different systems remains to be fully investigated, it is essential to note that they cannot account for the now well established, but widespread, post-transcriptional and translational repression that is elicited by glucocorticoids on inflammatory gene expression <citation rid="pone.0053936-Newton2" ref-type="bibr" pmid="10856322" doi="10.1136/thorax.55.7.603" pmcid="PMC1745805" count="1">[3]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0053936-Clark1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="22212616" doi="10.1016/j.pharmthera.2011.12.004" count="1">[6]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0053936-Stellato1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16113443" doi="10.1513/pats.200402-015MS" count="1">[25]</citation>.

In contrast to the above, we and many other investigators have noted that the ability of glucocorticoid to repress inflammatory gene expression is frequently prevented or attenuated by inhibition of transcription and/or translation (For examples see <citation rid="pone.0053936-Newton2" ref-type="bibr" pmid="10856322" doi="10.1136/thorax.55.7.603" pmcid="PMC1745805" count="1">[3]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0053936-Clark1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="22212616" doi="10.1016/j.pharmthera.2011.12.004" count="1">[6]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0053936-Stellato1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16113443" doi="10.1513/pats.200402-015MS" count="1">[25]</citation>). <sentence_start/>Rather than implying roles for “direct” mechanisms of transrepression, such data suggest that glucocorticoids induce the expression of “anti-inflammatory” genes to promote the repression of inflammatory gene expression <citation rid="pone.0053936-Clark1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="22212616" doi="10.1016/j.pharmthera.2011.12.004" count="1">[6]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0053936-Clark2" ref-type="bibr" pmid="17561338" doi="10.1016/j.mce.2007.04.013" count="1">[26]</citation>. <sentence_start/>In this respect, glucocorticoids induce the expression of very many genes, for example NFKBIA, in multiple cell types <citation rid="pone.0053936-Newton4" ref-type="bibr" pmid="17622575" doi="10.1124/mol.107.038794" count="1">[27]</citation>. <sentence_start/>While many such genes may play roles in the development of side-effects, it is clear that genes including mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) phosphatase (MKP) 1 (DUSP1) or glucocorticoid-induced leucine zipper protein (GILZ) (TSC22D3) show biological properties that are consistent with repression of inflammatory gene expression <citation rid="pone.0053936-Clark3" ref-type="bibr" pmid="18541529" doi="10.1074/jbc.R700053200" pmcid="PMC3258850" count="1">[28]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0053936-Ayroldi1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="19567371" doi="10.1096/fj.09-134684" count="1">[29]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Thus DUSP1 is rapidly and robustly induced by glucocorticoids and may inactivate all three major MAPK pathways to reduce inflammatory responses via transcriptional, post-transcriptional, translational and post-translational effects <citation rid="pone.0053936-Newton4" ref-type="bibr" pmid="17622575" doi="10.1124/mol.107.038794" count="1">[27]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0053936-Clark3" ref-type="bibr" pmid="18541529" doi="10.1074/jbc.R700053200" pmcid="PMC3258850" count="1">[28]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0053936-Kassel1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="11742987" doi="10.1093/emboj/20.24.7108" pmcid="PMC125780" count="1">[30]</citation>-<citation rid="pone.0053936-Issa1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="17513787" doi="10.4049/jimmunol.178.11.7366" count="1">[32]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Equally, TSC22D3 expression is increased in the lungs of asthmatics taking inhaled glucocorticoid, is variously described as a repressor of both AP-1 and NF-κB, and may also attenuate MAPK signalling <citation rid="pone.0053936-Kelly1" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1476-5381.2011.01620.x" pmcid="PMC3372826" pmid="21827450" count="1">[33]</citation>-<citation rid="pone.0053936-Ayroldi3" ref-type="bibr" pmid="17492054" doi="10.1172/JCI30724" pmcid="PMC1865030" count="1">[37]</citation>.

The above indicates multiple mechanisms of glucocorticoid repression that may either be independent of a requirement for gene expression (i.e. classical transrepression) or dependent on gene expression (i.e. repression via the transactivation of anti-inflammatory genes). <sentence_start/>To explore contributions due to these (potentially competing) hypotheses, we examined the effect of the synthetic glucocorticoid, dexamethasone, on 39 inflammatory gene transcripts whose expression was induced by IL-1β, a representative inflammatory stimulus, in human pulmonary A549 cells. <sentence_start/>Since A549 cells and primary human bronchial epithelial cells both show enhanced inflammatory gene expression in the presence of IL-1β and repression by glucocorticoid <citation rid="pone.0053936-Newton1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="19932713" doi="10.1016/j.pharmthera.2009.11.003" count="1">[2]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0053936-Kwon1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="8206512" pmcid="PMC1422337" count="1">[38]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0053936-Newton5" ref-type="bibr" pmid="12063092" doi="10.1016/s0014-2999(01)01624-7" count="1">[39]</citation>, these cells represent a valid model to examine the relationship between repression by dexamethasone and the roles of transactivation and transrepression. <sentence_start/>In addition, the central role of NF-κB in transrepression models, led us to interrogate the role of this factor in the expression of IL-1β-induced genes.
Materials and Methods
Cell Culture and Drugs

A549 cells were grown to confluence in Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (DMEM) supplemented with 10% fetal calf serum and L-glutamine (all Invitrogen). <sentence_start/>Cells were incubated overnight in serum-free medium prior to the addition of fresh serum-free medium containing cytokine and drugs. <sentence_start/>IL-1β (R&D systems) was dissolved in phosphate-buffered saline plus 0.1% bovine serum albumin (both Sigma), dexamethasone (Sigma) was dissolved in Hanks’ balanced salt solution (HBSS), cycloheximide (Sigma) was dissolved in sterile water and (gift from Dr. Ard Peeters, Organon Laboratories, The Netherlands) was dissolved in DMSO. <sentence_start/>Final concentrations of DMSO were <0.1%.
siRNA-mediated Gene Silencing

A549 cells at ∼60-70% confluence in 12 well plates were transfected with siRNAs. <sentence_start/>GR or control siRNA was mixed with Lipofectamine™ RNAi max (Invitrogen) (1 µg) in 100 µl of serum-free DMEM and then incubated at room temperature for 30 min. <sentence_start/>This mixture was then incubated on cells for 24 h at 37°C at a final siRNA concentration of 25 nM. <sentence_start/>Sequences for siRNA targeting were as follows: GR siRNA 6 (5′-AAGTGCAAACCTGCTGTGTTT-3′); Lamin siRNA (control) (5′-AACTGGACTTCCAGAAGAACA -3′) (both Qiagen).
Adenoviral Infection, Luciferase Reporters and Assay

A549 cells at ∼70% confluence were incubated for 24 h in DMEM plus 10% fetal calf serum containing the indicated multiplicity of infection (MOI) of adenoviral serotype 5 (Ad5) vector, prior to incubating in serum-free medium overnight and then experimental treatments. <sentence_start/>Ad5-IκBαΔN encodes a dominant version of IκBα, while Ad5-NF-κB-luc contains five copies of the classical NF-κB motif <citation rid="pone.0053936-Catley1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16687566" doi="10.1124/mol.106.023150" count="1">[40]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Ad5-NF-κB-luc was introduced into A549 cells at a MOI of 1 and cells were harvested in 1× reporter lysis buffer (Biotium) 6 h after the addition of IL-1β. <sentence_start/>Luminescence was measured using a 20/20n Luminometer (Turner Biosystems).
Western Blotting

Size-fractionation on 12% acrylamide gels, electroblotting to Hybond-ECL membranes (GE Healthcare) and immunodetection using ECL (Thermo Scientific) was as previously described <citation rid="pone.0053936-King1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="19648110" doi="10.1074/jbc.M109.028381" pmcid="PMC2785369" count="1">[41]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Antibodies were: anti-IκBα/MAD-3 (M-18) (sc-1102, Santa Cruz), anti-GR (sc-8992, Santa Cruz) and anti-glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (GAPDH) (4699-9555(ST), AbD Serotec).
RNA Isolation, cDNA Synthesis and SYBR Green Real-time PCR

RNA was isolated and 0.5 µg reverse transcribed into cDNA <citation rid="pone.0053936-King1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="19648110" doi="10.1074/jbc.M109.028381" pmcid="PMC2785369" count="1">[41]</citation>. <sentence_start/>After 1∶4 dilution, PCR was carried out on 2.5 µl of cDNA using SYBR GreenER mastermix (Invitrogen) and an ABI 7900HT instrument (Applied Biosystems). <sentence_start/>Relative cDNA concentrations were obtained from standard curves generated by serial dilution of an IL-1β-treated sample. <sentence_start/>Amplification conditions were: 50°C for 2 min, 95°C for 10 min then 40 cycles of 95°C for 15 s, 60°C for 1 min. <sentence_start/>For primer sequences see Table S1. <sentence_start/>Primer specificity was determined using dissociation (melt) curve analysis: 95°C for 15 s, 60°C for 20 s followed by ramping to 95°C over 20 min. <sentence_start/>A single peak in the change in fluorescence was taken to indicate specificity.
Statistical Analysis

All numerical values are expressed to two significant figures. <sentence_start/>Graphical data are plotted as mean ± S.E. Statistical analysis between groups was performed using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with a Bonferroni’s or Dunnet’s post test or a paired <italic toggle="yes">t</italic> test as indicated. <sentence_start/>Significance was assumed where: *, <italic toggle="yes">p</italic><0.05; **, <italic toggle="yes">p</italic><0.01; ***, <italic toggle="yes">p</italic><0.001.
Results
Effect of IL-1β and Dexamethasone on Inflammatory Gene Expression

To identify genes whose expression was induced by IL-1β and modulated by dexamethasone, A549 cells were treated with maximally effective concentrations of IL-1β (1 ng/ml) and/or dexamethasone (1 µM). <sentence_start/>As we have described <citation rid="pone.0053936-Chivers1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16988013" doi="10.1124/mol.106.025841" count="1">[42]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0053936-Kaur1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="17901197" doi="10.1124/mol.107.040121" count="1">[43]</citation>, cells were harvested after 6 and 18 h and RNA subjected to microarray analysis using Affymetrix U95Av2 and B chips. <sentence_start/>This revealed 428 genes that were induced by >2-fold by IL-1β at 6 h (Table S2). <sentence_start/>While a small number of these IL-1β-induced genes, for example NFKBIA, PRIC285 and BIRC3, showed modest mRNA inducibility by dexamethasone alone, the majority revealed either no effect or repression of basal expression (Table S2, Figure S1). <sentence_start/>In the presence of IL-1β for either 6 or 18 h, heat maps of IL-1β-induced genes with ≥4 fold inducibility at 6 h showed the response to dexamethasone to vary in a gene-dependent manner with the overall effect of dexamethasone favouring repression (Figure S1A). <sentence_start/>As depicted in Figure S1C (Groups 1-5), three of these IL-1β-induced genes (SERPINA3, LOC645638, APOL1) revealed enhanced (≥1.25 fold) expression in the presence of dexamethasone (Group 1). <sentence_start/>In group 2, there were 38 genes showing either no, or modest (<1.25/≥0.75 fold), modulation of IL-1β-induced expression by dexamethasone, whereas groups 3, 4 and 5 contained genes with increasing repression by dexamethasone (Figure S1C). <sentence_start/>However, there was no significant relationship between the fold induction by IL-1β and the repression achieved by dexamethasone. <sentence_start/>(Figure S1D).

To explore the regulation of IL-1β-induced genes by dexamethasone, 34 of the 35 genes corresponding to Affymetrix probe sets that individually showed >10-fold enhancement by IL-1β at 6 h were selected for analysis by real-time PCR (Table S2, Figure S1B). <sentence_start/>At the time of our analysis, the gene, c15orf48, was poorly annotated, did not show repression by dexamethasone (Figure S1A) and was not analysed. <sentence_start/>In addition, four commonly studied inflammatory genes, GM-CSF (CSF2), COX-2 (PTGS2), IL-1β (IL1B) and TNFα (TNF), were also selected for analysis. <sentence_start/>In each case, a single primer pair crossing an exon/exon boundary was designed for each gene to amplify all RefSeq splice variants, with the exception of IFIT3, which has two splice variants with only one exon in common. <sentence_start/>Therefore, two primer pairs were designed for this gene and designated IFIT3iso1 and IFIT3iso2. <sentence_start/>A total of 39 mRNAs were subjected to real-time PCR analysis. <sentence_start/>A549 cells were treated with IL-1β and dexamethasone, either alone or in combination, for 1, 2, 6 or 18 h. <sentence_start/>The mRNA expression profiles for these 39 mRNAs were placed into three categories (early, intermediate and late - see figure legends for definitions) based on the timing of peak expression induced by IL-1β as represented by the line graphs in Figure 1A (for detailed information on each individual gene see Figure S2).

A549 cells were either not stimulated (NS) or treated with IL-1β (1 ng/ml), dexamethasone (dex) (1 µM) or a combination of the two for 1, 2, 6 and 18 h. <sentence_start/>Cells were then harvested for RNA and real-time PCR was carried out for the indicated genes and GAPDH. <sentence_start/>Data (n = 3), normalised to GAPDH are expressed as either log<sub>2</sub> fold over NS at 1 h (left panel) or as percentage of IL-1β (right hand panel) and plotted as means. <sentence_start/>Genes are grouped based on expression patterns: ‘Early-phase’ genes are those which have a peak of expression at 1 or 2 h (top two graphs); ‘Late-phase’ genes have a peak of expression at 6 h or later with less than 50% of that peak expression observed at 1 or 2 h (bottom two graphs); and ‘Intermediate’ genes are those that fall into neither of the above categories (middle two graphs). <sentence_start/><bold>B.</bold> <sentence_start/>Effect of dexamethasone from right hand panel of A is plotted at each time point for all genes repressed by dexamethasone. <sentence_start/>Significance was tested using one-way ANOVA with a Bonferroni post-test and is indicated: *, <italic toggle="yes">P</italic><0.05; ***, <italic toggle="yes">P</italic><0.001.

Of the 39 IL-1β-induced transcripts analysed by PCR, twelve, including PRIC285 and BIRC3, which were modestly dexamethasone induced in the array (Figure S1), showed two or more fold enhancement by dexamethasone alone for at least one time point (Table 1, Figure S2) and this effect was significant for seven genes. <sentence_start/>For example, dexamethasone induced CSF3 mRNA by up to 30 fold at all time points. <sentence_start/>Although lower in magnitude, similar responses were seen for BIRC3, TNFAIP3 and G0S2, thus identifying these genes as <italic toggle="yes">bona fides</italic> dexamethasone-induced genes. <sentence_start/>Conversely, and despite significant increases in mRNA for at least one time point, the effects on IFIT1, LAMB3 and PRIC285 were less consistent. <sentence_start/>While the functional relevance of these observations requires consideration, the induction by dexamethasone was considerably less than the maximal induction by IL-1β (Table 1).

In combination with IL-1β, dexamethasone showed varying effects on inflammatory gene expression (Figure 1, Figure S2). <sentence_start/>Analysis of the effect of 1 µM dexamethasone on IL-1β-induced mRNA at 6 h showed that 34 of the IL-1β-inducible mRNAs were significantly repressed by dexamethasone, whereas five genes, (BIRC3, CSF3, IL32, SOD2 and TNFAIP3) were not repressed (Figure 2). <sentence_start/>Furthermore, of the mRNAs repressed by dexamethasone, the majority showed increasing levels of repression with time, a trend which is readily seen in the line graphs in Figure 1A (for detailed information on individual genes see Figure S2). <sentence_start/>For example, at 1 h, repression of CCL2, CCL20, PTGS2 and others was minimal, yet increased markedly by 2 and 6 h (Figure S2). <sentence_start/>Indeed, after excluding the 5 genes not repressed by dexamethasone, the combined repression of all genes by dexamethasone was significantly greater at 2 h and 6 h when compared to 1 h (Figure 1B). <sentence_start/>Equally, the overall level of repression was significantly greater at 6 h compared to 2 h; thus, a clear time-dependence to the repression of most inflammatory genes by dexamethasone is established.

Effect of Dexamethasone Concentration on IL-1β-induced Gene Expression

For the remaining 21 IL-1β-induced mRNAs, cycloheximide had one of three effects on the repression elicited by dexamethasone. <sentence_start/>Cycloheximide significantly blocked the dexamethasone-dependent repression of 11 genes (Figure 5). <sentence_start/>These can be classified into two groups: i) mRNAs for which cycloheximide “fully reversed” the repression by dexamethasone (Figure 5A), and; ii) mRNAs where there was only a “partial reversal” of the dexamethasone-dependent repression by cycloheximide (Figure 5B). <sentence_start/>“Full reversal” was defined as where the percentage repression by dexamethasone was significantly reversed in the presence of cycloheximide and resulted in no significant repression, i.e. there was no difference from control (IL-1β plus cycloheximide). <sentence_start/>Similarly, “partial reversal” is when the percent repression by dexamethasone was significantly reversed by cycloheximide, but that this was still significantly repressed compared to control (IL-1β plus cycloheximide). <sentence_start/>i.e. repression still occurred, but to a lesser extent. <sentence_start/>Finally, there was a group of 10 mRNAs showing “no reversal” for which the presence of cycloheximide did not attenuate dexamethasone-induced repression (Figure 5C).

Discussion

The current study focuses on mechanisms underlying the ability of the anti-inflammatory glucocorticoid, dexamethasone, to repress the mRNA expression of inflammatory genes induced by IL-1β. <sentence_start/>Using Affymetrix HG-U95Av2 and B microarrays, just under 430 mRNAs were identified that were induced 2 fold or more by IL-1β (at 6 h). <sentence_start/>The effects of dexamethasone, in the presence of IL-1β, on these genes was highly variable, with a few genes showing further enhanced expression, many genes showing little effect of dexamethasone and the majority revealing reduced expression (Figure S1 and Table S2). <sentence_start/>This finding is supported by real-time PCR data showing repression for 34 out of 39 IL-1β-induced mRNAs. <sentence_start/>While the reversal of this dexamethasone-dependent repression by both a GR antagonist, , and GR-specific siRNA clearly supports a role for GR, it is equally clear that such reversals were often only partial. <sentence_start/>In the case of , this could be due to the nature of the effect of on GR. <sentence_start/>Thus on a low potency response such as the 2×GRE reporter (EC<sub>50</sub> for dexamethasone = 34 nM), acts as a competitive antagonist (Figure 3A). <sentence_start/>However, on higher potency responses, such as the repression of IL-1β-induced mRNAs (EC<sub>50</sub> values for Dex 0.7-10 nM), it is clear that can exert agonistic effects (Table S4). <sentence_start/>In such instances antagonism of the full agonist (dexamethasone) is limited to the extent of the agonism of the partial agonist ( ) (an effect referred to as competitive dualism). <sentence_start/>It is also important to note that the GR-specific siRNA does not completely prevent GR expression and this correlates with reduced, but not absent, 2×GRE-dependent transcription in the presence of the GR-specific siRNA (Figures 3B and 3C). <sentence_start/>Thus, low levels of GR may be sufficient for real-time PCR also revealed significant up-regulation of CSF3, G0S2, IFIT1, LAMB3 and TNFAIP3 by dexamethasone. <sentence_start/>Thus, it is possible that an independent ability of glucocorticoid to induce expression of such genes may help maintain IL-1β-induced expression in the presence of glucocorticoid, which may, in fact, also act to switch off many of the pathways that are activated by IL-1β. <sentence_start/>Certainly, CSF3, BIRC3, TNFAIP3 and G0S2 are IL-1β-induced genes that were the least affected by dexamethasone. <sentence_start/>Interestingly, IL32, which also falls into this group, was induced >2-fold by dexamethasone (although this effect did not reach significance). <sentence_start/>Such data illustrate a mechanism by which certain responses could be maintained in the context of increased glucocorticoids. <sentence_start/>Indeed, our array data confirms modest up-regulation of NFKBIA by dexamethasone, yet IL-1β-induced expression was unaffected by glucocorticoid, as previously shown <citation rid="pone.0053936-Newton3" ref-type="bibr" pmid="9652398" doi="10.1046/j.1432-1327.1998.2540081.x" count="1">[16]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Therefore the modest up-regulation of NFKB1A by glucocorticoids may aid in maintaining its expression, and therefore feedback control of NF-κB. <sentence_start/>Of note is the fact that we have observed an equivalent effect for the mRNA destabilising protein tristetraprolin (TTP) or ZFP36. <sentence_start/>This is primarily induced by IL-1β to exert feedback control of inflammatory genes, such as IL-8 and GM-CSF, and is only modestly induced by dexamethasone <citation rid="pone.0053936-King2" ref-type="bibr" pmid="19435930" doi="10.1124/jpet.109.151423" count="1">[59]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Hence we speculate that glucocorticoid-inducibility of a subset of inflammatory genes may help preserve various components of the inflammatory response, for example by maintaining aspects of host defence or necessary feedback regulation. <sentence_start/>Assuming transcriptional regulation for this modest glucocorticoid-inducibility, such data predict the existence of identifiable glucocorticoid responsive regions in the promoters of these inflammatory genes. <sentence_start/>Indeed, a study of GR binding sites in dexamethasone responsive genes found that both BIRC3 and TNFAIP3 are bound by GR within 10 kB of the transcription start site, consistent with up-regulation of these genes by dexamethasone in the current study <citation rid="pone.0053936-Reddy1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="19801529" doi="10.1101/gr.097022.109" pmcid="PMC2792167" count="1">[23]</citation>.

While real-time PCR analysis allowed the 39 IL-1β-induced mRNAs to be grouped according to expression kinetic (early, intermediate or late), we were not able to identify obvious differences in responsiveness to dexamethasone between these groups. <sentence_start/>All three groups contained genes whose expression was highly, lowly or partially repressed by dexamethasone in a GR-dependent manner. <sentence_start/>While, these groupings were merely based on temporal differences in expression, it was predicted that those genes revealing a delayed kinetic of induction (i.e. late phase) would represent genes whose expression depends on some time-dependent event, for example, the prior expression of another factor that was essential for expression. <sentence_start/>The fact that the protein synthesis inhibitor, cycloheximide, prevented or reduced expression of many of these late genes, yet none of the early genes were affected, supports this view. <sentence_start/>Equally, cycloheximide significantly blocked the expression of four genes (BCL2A1, G0S2, IL1B and TFF1) in the intermediate group, suggesting that their expression was also dependent on the synthesis of one or more new factors. <sentence_start/>All such cycloheximide-sensitive genes were necessarily excluded from the later parts of our analysis as the effect of inhibiting proteins synthesis on the repression by dexamethasone cannot be tested on genes whose expression is itself sensitive to protein synthesis inhibition. <sentence_start/>Thus the main findings of our study are restricted to acute phase genes whose expression induced by IL-1β was not attenuate by blockade of protein synthesis.

Possibly the most surprising and important finding to come out of the current study was the correlation between potency (EC<sub>50</sub>) of repression by dexamethasone with the extent of repression. <sentence_start/>While variation in these parameters was obvious and intuitive, it was unexpected that a correlation would exist such that IL-1β-induced genes showing the greatest repression by dexamethasone were also the most potently repressed by dexamethasone. <sentence_start/>This result suggests that in the context of a sub-maximal level of glucocorticoid, such as may occur in patients undergoing inhaled glucocorticoid therapy in the treatment of asthma, these would represent the most sensitive genes to repression by glucocorticoids and may therefore represent the main drivers of the response to therapy. <sentence_start/>Equally, this implies that mechanisms induced by the glucocorticoid and which cause this repression must also be active at such concentrations of glucocorticoid. <sentence_start/>If the effects of protein synthesis inhibition are now considered, these data reveal that the IL-1β-induced genes whose expression was repressed by dexamethasone in a cycloheximide-sensitive manner are the genes most repressed and most potently repressed by dexamethasone. <sentence_start/>Thus, a requirement for ongoing gene expression in these repressive events is implicated and this is consistent with prior studies that implicated the repression of PTGS2, CXCL1, IL6, IL8 and CSF2 as being at least partially dependent on glucocorticoid-induced expression of DUSP1 or TSC22D3 <citation rid="pone.0053936-Lasa1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="12391149" doi="10.1128/MCB.22.22.7802-7811.2002" pmcid="PMC134716" count="1">[31]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0053936-Issa1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="17513787" doi="10.4049/jimmunol.178.11.7366" count="1">[32]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0053936-Eddleston1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="17208592" doi="10.1016/j.jaci.2006.08.027" count="1">[36]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0053936-Quante1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="18314542" doi="10.1165/rcmb.2007-0014OC" count="1">[60]</citation>-<citation rid="pone.0053936-Newton6" ref-type="bibr" pmid="20100175" doi="10.1042/BJ20091038" count="1">[62]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Hence, the ability to prevent the repressive effects of dexamethasone with cycloheximide is consistent with repression occurring via the glucocorticoid-dependent expression of repressive genes, i.e. requires transactivation by GR. <sentence_start/>As such, the induction of DUSP1 occurs with an EC<sub>50</sub> in the low nanomolar range, a potency similar to the repression of the most sensitively repressed inflammatory genes <citation rid="pone.0053936-King1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="19648110" doi="10.1074/jbc.M109.028381" pmcid="PMC2785369" count="1">[41]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, many glucocorticoid-induced genes reveal even greater potencies (low EC<sub>50</sub>) and this suggests that repression occurring via the induction of anti-inflammatory genes is highly plausible <citation rid="pone.0053936-Reddy1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="19801529" doi="10.1101/gr.097022.109" pmcid="PMC2792167" count="1">[23]</citation>. <sentence_start/>As noted above, late phase genes were excluded from this analysis due to their expression being inhibited in the presence of cycloheximide. <sentence_start/>This meant that the role of glucocorticoid-inducible genes could only be examined in respect of early phase genes. <sentence_start/>Whether this introduces an unintentional bias into the results of these experiments is unclear. <sentence_start/>However, it is likely that late phase genes would also be inhibited by a combination of mechanisms, especially considering that there are both genes whose expression is highly or lowly repressed by dexamethasone in this group, as is seen with the early phase group.

Equally, the IL-1β-induced genes which show cycloheximide-dependent repression are those genes for which a strong time-dependence to their repression is observed (Figure 6F). <sentence_start/>This suggests a need for time-dependent processes, such as new gene expression, to occur prior to the onset of repression. <sentence_start/>Conversely, genes not showing a cycloheximide-dependent component to the repression by dexamethasone are consistent with a conventional transrepressive mechanism. <sentence_start/>This mechanism does not involve a gene expression-dependent event, but rather is reported to occur via a direct interaction with GR and the recruitment of HDAC activity to targeted promoters <citation rid="pone.0053936-Ito2" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16380507" doi="10.1084/jem.20050466" pmcid="PMC2118081" count="1">[63]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Interestingly, this group of genes does not display time-dependent repression (Figure 6F) and is consistent with a rapid onset of repression due to GR recruitment. <sentence_start/>Finally, it is important to realise that a number of genes revealed both cycloheximide-sensitive and -insensitive components to their repression by dexamethasone. <sentence_start/>This suggests that these inflammatory genes are subject to repression via both GR transactivation and transrepression. <sentence_start/>Given recent findings that implicate the glucocorticoid induction of DUSP1 in the repression of both AP-1 and NF-κB <citation rid="pone.0053936-King1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="19648110" doi="10.1074/jbc.M109.028381" pmcid="PMC2785369" count="1">[41]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0053936-Diefenbacher1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="18535250" doi="10.1210/me.2007-0574" pmcid="PMC2505324" count="1">[64]</citation>, both targets of classical transrepression <citation rid="pone.0053936-DeBosscher1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="12920152" doi="10.1210/er.2002-0006" count="1">[5]</citation>, it is perhaps not surprising that at least some mRNAs show glucocorticoid-dependent repression that involves both classical GR transrepression and transactivation. <sentence_start/>Thus, there exists considerable possibility for redundancy both between and within these two mechanisms of repression. <sentence_start/>In this regard, multiple mechanisms of transrepression are established <citation rid="pone.0053936-DeBosscher1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="12920152" doi="10.1210/er.2002-0006" count="1">[5]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Likewise, NFKB1A, TSC22D3 and DUSP1 and others are up-regulated by glucocorticoids and may all impact on pathways involved in inflammatory gene expression <citation rid="pone.0053936-Newton4" ref-type="bibr" pmid="17622575" doi="10.1124/mol.107.038794" count="1">[27]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Moreover, cycloheximide would not prevent the effect of induced RNAs, for example microRNA (miRNA), in the repression of inflammatory gene expression. <sentence_start/>It is therefore possible that glucocorticoids, by inducing miRNA expression, could then inhibit inflammatory gene expression.

In conclusion, our data show that a single, global mechanism of inflammatory gene repression does not account for all of the anti-inflammatory actions of glucocorticoids. <sentence_start/>Indeed, more gene-specific methods of inhibition that could involve transrepressive and/or transactivation mechanisms of repression are indicated. <sentence_start/>Importantly, the inhibition of inflammatory genes that are highly repressed by glucocorticoids appears to involve the induction of anti-inflammatory gene expression and occurs at low concentrations of glucocorticoid. <sentence_start/>These data highlight the importance of GR-induced transactivation for the effective repression of inflammatory gene expression by glucocorticoids.
